subject: Computer Networking
title: Tim Berners-Lee Invents the Web
description: A fast breakdown of Tim Berners-Lee Invents the Web for builders.

hook.text: In 1989 at CERN, a physicist wanted a better way to share documents. He invented the World Wide Web.

buildup.text: Tim Berners-Lee created three things: HTML for pages, HTTP for transfer, and URLs for addressing.

discovery.text: His first web page went live on August 6, 1991. It explained what the web was and how to use it.

twist.text: CERN made the web free for everyone. If they had patented it, the web might have become a paid service.

climax.text: Within five years, the web went from a physics tool to the most popular service on the internet.

punchline.text: One physicist's side project became the world's information platform.

quiz.question: What three technologies did Tim Berners-Lee create for the web?

details.summary: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989, creating HTML, HTTP, and URLs. His system made internet content accessible through linked documents that anyone could publish and browse. CERN released the technology freely, enabling the explosive growth of the web.
details.whyItMatters: The web transformed the internet from a tool for specialists into a platform for everyone. By making information linkable and browsable, Berners-Lee created the information age.
takeaways: Berners-Lee created HTML, HTTP, and URLs at CERN in 1989
The web made internet content accessible to non-technical users
CERN's decision to release it freely enabled global adoption

faq.question: What problem was Berners-Lee trying to solve?
faq.answer: CERN researchers needed to share documents across different computer systems. Berners-Lee proposed a system of interlinked hypertext documents accessible over the network. His solution combined hypertext, the internet, and a simple markup language into the web we know today.

faq.question: Why was CERN's free release so important?
faq.answer: If CERN had patented or licensed the web technologies, adoption would have been slow and fragmented. By releasing HTML, HTTP, and the web server software freely in 1993, anyone could create websites and browsers. This openness enabled the explosive growth of the web.
